clue.text: The expression of some cur given a suspended sentence?

definitions.text: The expression of some cur given a suspended sentence?

parts.words: The expression of some cur given a suspended sentence?
parts.note: a 'suspended sentence' read as hanging: the look on the face of a cur about to be hanged, a shamefaced, guilty expression

explanation.surface: A mongrel's face as it is let off by the court with a suspended sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: A suspended sentence in court means no jail, but here 'suspended' means hanged, and a dog facing the noose looks downcast and guilty.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a guilty, shamefaced look, the expression worn by someone abject or cowed.

clue.text: Turning head-to tail, whacks a metal cutter

indicators.note: the head letter of the words is turned round to sit at the tail, moving the first letter to the end

parts.note: the clue words taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone spins round and strikes a tool used for cutting metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning head-to tail' moves the first letter, W, of WHACKSA to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw with a fine-toothed blade in a frame is the standard hand tool for cutting through metal.

clue.text: Look. Royal Naval force involved in East Anglia

indicators.note: involved means tangled or mixed up, so these letters are jumbled together

parts.note: taken as the word itself
RN is the abbreviation for Royal Navy, Royal Naval
F is the physics abbreviation for force

explanation.surface: An order to look as naval forces take part in an exercise on the East Anglian coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' jumbles LOOK, RN and F. East Anglia is the region of eastern England made up chiefly of the counties of Norfolk and Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: The county is one of the two main shires making up that eastern English region, so it lies there.

clue.text: The tendency to go with the stream

explanation.surface: Someone's habit of conforming and following the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Drift is the general tendency or gist of something, and as a verb it means to be carried along by a current.

clue.text: The sort of guard to disperse danger? That is right

indicators.note: dispersing scatters the letters of the word danger into a new arrangement

parts.note: i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is

explanation.surface: A guard whose job is to drive danger away, and quite rightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to disperse' rearranges DANGER into GRENAD, then IE and R follow. The Grenadier Guards are a regiment of the British Army's Foot Guards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grenadier Guards are a famous regiment of household troops, so a soldier of that regiment is that sort of guard.

clue.text: Room for such clever tricks!

parts.note: small conjuring feats done to entertain guests at home are named after the sitting room where they were performed

explanation.surface: A space suited to a magician's clever turns.
explanation.walkthrough: Parlour tricks are small party conjuring stunts, named after the old-fashioned front sitting room where guests were entertained.
explanation.definitionFit: A parlour is a sitting room, and the tricks performed to amuse visitors there take its name.

clue.text: Wept when welcomed aboard

explanation.surface: Someone was moved to tears on being greeted as they came on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipe one's eye' is an old phrase for weep; a ship's bosun pipes dignitaries aboard with a whistle call.
explanation.definitionFit: To pipe is an old word for cry or weep, and naval honour guards greet visitors on deck with a boatswain's whistle.

clue.text: The jewellery a fake? That could sound unbelievable

explanation.surface: Doubts about whether a piece of jewellery is genuine, and a story that does not convince.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes the words literally: the band on a finger is not genuine. The second is the idiom for a claim that seems untrue.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, a counterfeit band; as an idiom, said of a statement that strikes the listener as untrue or insincere.

clue.text: A judgment on first work I turn in

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work

indicators.note: turn means the short word in is spun round to read backwards

parts.note: taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: A ruling delivered on the first piece of work handed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses IN to NI; 'first' tells you OP, I and NI come before ON, which the clue prints first.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion is a considered view or verdict, such as a judge's or expert's judgment.

clue.text: Renounce a slice of the serene Guernsey countryside

indicators.note: a slice is a piece cut from inside the phrase, so the letters run within these words

explanation.surface: Turning one's back on a peaceful stretch of the Channel Island's countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a slice of' takes the letters running across sereNE GUErnsey. Renegue is a variant spelling of renege.
explanation.definitionFit: To renegue is to go back on a promise or deny a commitment, the same as reneging.

clue.text: The red carriage brought to the pit

parts.note: a car is a railway carriage or a motor carriage
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: A red-painted railway wagon is hauled to the coal pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Carmine is a deep crimson pigment, a shade of red.

clue.text: It's supposed to cover meals and bed, but the retired might question it

definitions.text: It's supposed to cover meals and bed

explanation.surface: A boarding rate that pensioners grumble about.
explanation.walkthrough: A pension, as on the Continent, is a boarding house or the board-and-lodging rate it charges; the retired live on the other sense, their pension, and may query its size.
explanation.definitionFit: In European use it is a guesthouse charge covering room and food; it is also the regular income paid after retirement.

clue.text: A below-average worker used for getting things down quickly

definitions.text: used for getting things down quickly

parts.note: short means below average height or length
a hand is a manual worker, as on a farm

explanation.surface: An undersized labourer is taken on to rush through a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting things down' means writing them down, not lowering them.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorthand is a system of abbreviated symbols for taking dictation fast in writing.

clue.text: Complete freedom for cast

explanation.surface: Total liberty given to the actors in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a noun for actors but is the verb throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A full fling is a spell of unrestrained indulgence, and to fling something is to throw or hurl it.

clue.text: Rouses himself for the factory holiday

explanation.surface: A worker gets himself up for the annual mill holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Wakes Week was the annual summer holiday when the mills and factories of northern England shut down.
explanation.definitionFit: To wake is to rouse from sleep; the wakes were the traditional annual mill-town closures for a week of holiday.

clue.text: A big killing from reprinting rough tales, nothing omitted

indicators.note: reprinting the words sets their letters in a new order
omitted means the letter for nothing is dropped from the word rough

parts.note: O, the round figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: Rough stories reissued in full, telling of a great massacre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'omitted' drops O from ROUGH to give RUGH; 'reprinting' rearranges RUGH with TALES. 'A big killing' suggests a financial windfall, but here it is a massacre.
explanation.definitionFit: Slaughter is the killing of many people or animals at once, a massacre.

clue.text: Nothing is heard about how some Brotherhoods work

explanation.surface: Silent orders of monks, where no word is spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: Some religious brotherhoods, like Trappist monks, keep a rule of silence.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means without any sound, and enclosed orders that keep a vow of silence carry out their work without speaking.

clue.text: In an undertone, as the Italians might say

definitions.text: In an undertone, as the Italians might say

parts.words: In an undertone, as the Italians might say
parts.note: the clue asks for the Italian phrase meaning in a quiet voice, literally under the voice

explanation.surface: Speaking quietly, in the manner of the Italians.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is Italian for 'under the voice', and is used in English, especially in music, for speaking or singing softly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian expression means quietly, in a lowered voice, which is the English sense of in an undertone.

clue.text: Crude root vegetable strung up for donkey-work

explanation.surface: An uncooked vegetable dangled in front of a working beast.
explanation.walkthrough: A carrot dangled on a string in front of a donkey keeps it plodding on; 'crude' here means uncooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncooked, the orange root is a crude vegetable; hung before a donkey, it is the lure that keeps the animal working.

clue.text: Immersed the lot in water grass and started again

indicators.note: something immersed is plunged inside, so one piece is put within the other

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass growing in water
a sum is a total, the lot

explanation.surface: Someone dunked everything among the reeds and then carried on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Immersed ... in' puts SUM inside REED.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to begin again after a pause, so resumed means picked up again.

clue.text: A Royal Society whip-round for the Prince of Wales as was?

definitions.text: the Prince of Wales as was?

indicators.note: round means the word whip goes around the other letters, enclosing them

parts.note: taken as the word itself
RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society, Britain's scientific academy

explanation.surface: Fellows of a learned society hold a collection for the heir to the throne of old.
explanation.walkthrough: A whip-round is a collection, but here 'round' puts WHIP around A RS. HMS Prince of Wales was a Royal Navy battleship sunk in 1941.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Prince of Wales was a battleship, a fighting vessel of the Royal Navy, now gone, hence 'as was'.

clue.text: Borders of sedges

indicators.note: of signals that the answer is a part taken out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: The margins of a patch of marsh plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The word as printed, 'sedge', lacks the final S that the answer needs; read 'sedges', whose letters after the first S give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Borders and edges are both the outer margins or rims of something.

clue.text: Yielded up when taking fresh tot in the dance

indicators.note: taking means holding something within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: gave up means yielded, so gave is yielded

indicators.note: fresh means new or remade, so the word tot is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone surrendered on being handed a new tot of drink at the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' rearranges TOT to OTT, and 'when taking' puts it inside GAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: The gavotte is an old French court dance in moderate four-time.

clue.text: Deviated, yet could be ready to follow holy man

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for saint, a holy man

indicators.note: could be signals that the word ready may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone went astray, though they might have been prepared to follow a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges READY to RAYED, and 'to follow' puts it after ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who strayed wandered off course, departing from the right path.

clue.text: Twig what the embroidery represents

explanation.surface: A small branch pictured in needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twig' could be the slang verb for understand, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig is a small shoot or spray of a plant, and also a decorative design of such a spray worked in fabric.

clue.text: Explain away garbled distress message held by hand-covering operator

indicators.note: held by means one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: a glover is a maker of gloves, a worker in hand-coverings

indicators.note: garbled means jumbled, so the letters of the distress call are scrambled

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal

explanation.surface: A radio operator wearing gloves sends a muddled call for help that needs explaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garbled' turns SOS into SSO, and 'held by' places it inside GLOVER. 'Operator' hints at a radio operator but means a tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: To gloss over a fault is to make light of it, explaining it away or hiding it.

clue.text: Pass information on hashish

explanation.surface: Telling the authorities about some cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: To grass is British slang for informing on someone to the police; grass is also slang for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform on someone to the police is slang to grass, and the word is also slang for marijuana or similar drugs.

clue.text: Bundle unnamed lady to a French capital

parts.note: she is a pronoun standing for a woman not named

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

parts.note: the capital, or first letter, of French is F

explanation.surface: A woman with no name is bundled off to Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French capital' suggests Paris, but it means the capital letter of French.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheaf is a bundle, as of corn stalks or papers tied together.

clue.text: Revered Buddhist mothers with one head-dress between them

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
a hat is a head-dress
the second mother, again ma

explanation.surface: Two mothers sharing a single hat, revered by Buddhists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'between them' puts HAT between the two MAs. Mahatma means great soul, a title for a revered sage.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma is a title of honour for a holy sage held in deep reverence, as in Indian religions.

clue.text: Frankly, love, try to get reorganised

indicators.note: reorganised means arranged in a new order, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: An honest plea to a sweetheart to sort themselves out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get reorganised' rearranges LOVE and TRY. 'Love' looks like an endearment but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtly means openly, without concealment, as does frankly.

clue.text: Into small departments some fine painting goes

indicators.note: into means one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: depts is the short form of departments

indicators.note: some means only part of the word is used, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: art covers fine painting

explanation.surface: Good pictures are hung in the little sections of a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' trims ART to AR, and 'Into' puts AR inside DEPTS, the short form of departments.
explanation.definitionFit: Departs and goes both mean leaves or sets off.

clue.text: Rifle a settlement of Greater London

explanation.surface: A gun and a borough on the north side of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lee-Enfield rifle was made at Enfield, a north London borough.
explanation.definitionFit: The Enfield rifle was the British service weapon, named after the north London borough where it was made.
